Tehran sets out terms as US-Iran talks intensify in New York

Iran formally set out its conditions for ending the war as indirect talks with the United States intensified in New York on Tuesday, with the Strait of Hormuz and Washington's naval blockade emerging as central points in efforts to turn renewed contacts into an agreement.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said Iran conveyed its conditions to the United States through a Qatari mediator in New York. They included an end to the war on all fronts, a halt to what Tehran described as US "acts of aggression," an end to the naval blockade and economic warfare, and the release of Iranian assets.
US special envoy Steve Witkoff said mediators shuttled between American and Iranian delegations throughout the day and that the two sides completed a round of discussions he hoped would prove "constructive and promising."
The talks coincided with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's arrival in New York for the General Assembly.
Reuters reported that a senior Iranian official said Tehran could reopen Hormuz within seven days if Washington eased military pressure and lifted its blockade on Iranian ports.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said she and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi discussed ending the war and fully reopening Hormuz, arguing that navigation should be free and unimpeded and that there should be no tolls or fees after the war.
French President Emmanuel Macron also said reopening the strait was the "main objective" of his Monday talks with US President Donald Trump. Macron said the situation in Hormuz had been "probably underestimated" and that France was prepared to become more involved in enabling transit while avoiding a direct confrontation.
Al Arabiya reported, citing a US source who attended a meeting with the Iranian delegation, that Washington had rejected Iran's request to lift the blockade and that major obstacles to an agreement remained.
Trump said Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held a "very good" three-hour meeting with an Iranian delegation and predicted that "a settlement is going to be reached."
Iranian state television later confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Witkoff "at the insistence of the American side" and conveyed Tehran's conditions.
During Trump's meeting with Persian Gulf Arab and other regional leaders, he said Witkoff and Jared Kushner had also held a "very productive" meeting with mediators working on Iran.
"I think there's a lot of momentum for them to make a deal," Trump said, adding that his envoys had respect on both sides and that he believed they would "get this thing ended."

Hormuz moves to center of negotiations
In the meeting with Witkoff, Araghchi presented Iran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, including lifting the US naval blockade, releasing frozen Iranian assets and ending the war across all "resistance" fronts, according to state media.
A senior Iranian official separately told Reuters that Tehran could reopen the strait within seven days if Washington eased military pressure and lifted the blockade on Iranian ports. The proposal was conveyed to the United States through mediators last week, the official said, adding that Iran's delegation in New York had authority to pursue renewed diplomacy.
Parliament deputy speaker Ali Nikzad said negotiations were now tied to Hormuz and that Iran would "not back down" over the strait.
A parliamentary committee, meanwhile, advanced provisions allowing authorities to seize 20% of the cargo or its value from ships found to have violated Iranian passage rules.

Regional push gathers pace
Qatar said Tuesday it was working with Pakistan to open a path for dialogue and facilitate an agreement between Tehran and Washington, including a possible short-term deal that could allow wider negotiations to resume.
Araghchi met Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani in New York on Tuesday.
Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Pakistan and Turkey also called for dialogue and diplomacy and backed implementation of the Islamabad memorandum between Iran and the United States.
Trump said Washington was "hearing from everybody" and compared the gathering with a similar meeting last year that preceded the Gaza agreement.

Threats remain around diplomacy
Trump used his UN address to urge other countries to join Washington's campaign to isolate Iran and later warned Tehran to act "fast" before it was too late.
During his meeting with GCC leaders, he also threatened another strike on Pickaxe Mountain if the United States detected renewed activity there.
"We may have to blow up another one, Pickaxe Mountain. We're not seeing a lot of activity there, but if we do, we'll blow it up immediately," he said.
IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi said the force did not reject diplomacy but viewed negotiations as a way to impose Iran's conditions. Iran's top military commands separately warned of "more severe, crushing and unpredictable" strikes if the United States or Israel attacked again.
After saying at the UN that an agreement might come after the US midterm elections, he told regional leaders it could happen "maybe before."

Prospects of Pezeshkian-Trump meeting
President Masoud Pezeshkian is in New York for the General Assembly, but no meeting with Trump has been announced yet. Iranian officials say Pezeshkian does not plan to meet Trump, despite the US president saying he would be open to one.
Pezeshkian, speaking aboard a plane to New York for the UN General Assembly, said on Tuesday he wanted the assembly to help bring an end to "war and bloodshed" and restore trust in the world.
"We will use this opportunity in the best possible way to convey Iran's message of victimhood to the international community," he said before departing.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who arrived in New York ahead of Pezeshkian, said Iran remained in a "state of war" following US-Israeli attacks and subsequent developments.
"The question of restoring trust is important and provides an opportunity to discuss with the world how trust in the United Nations was lost and how it can be restored," Araghchi said.
IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi: "If the country's interests require it, negotiations can be part of the battle while we remain prepared for combat," Mohebbi said. "One war is fought with weapons; in negotiations, the war is fought with words, arguments and diplomatic methods." ... "The war is not over," he said.
Lawmaker Mohammad Rostami said any direct negotiations with Trump would be unacceptable, calling the US president the "killer of our martyred leader."
Saudi Arabia restarted its East-West oil pipeline and could resume crude exports from the Red Sea port of Yanbu later Tuesday, Reuters reported.
Beijing has offered to help Washington press Iran over the war in return for US concessions on arms sales to Taiwan, Reuters reported, citing sources familiar with discussions between the US and China ahead of a meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
